s: Part two.
Structured error responses.
By the end of this part, you'll know which of two channels a failure belongs in.
The four classes of execution error, and what each one tells the agent to do.
And how one error can serve both the model and your code.
Here's the picture.
You send someone to the pharmacy for you.
They come back empty-handed.
"It didn't work" tells you nothing.
But four other answers each change what should happen next.
One.
The shop was shut, and opens at nine.
So going back later works.
Two.
They don't stock it, and won't for a month.
So the errand itself needs rethinking.
Three.
They won't release that prescription to anyone but you.
So no amount of persistence helps.
Someone with standing has to step in.
Four.
The address you wrote down doesn't exist.
So the errand was broken before it started.
An agent reading a tool failure is standing in exactly that hallway.
With one difference.
It will act on whatever you tell it, immediately.
And it has no instinct that stops it going back to a closed shop forty times.
So what's a structured error for?
It makes three messages legible to something that cannot infer them.
"Come back later."
"This will never work, do something else."
And "I am not allowed."
First concept.
The two channels.
Picture a kitchen that gets two kinds of bad tickets.
Some are unreadable, or ask for a dish that isn't on the menu.
The cook sends those straight back to the front desk.
Others are perfectly clear, but ask for something that can't be done today.
Those go back with a note, explaining what the diner can have instead.
In M C P terms, the first kind is a protocol error.
M C P messages travel in a format called JSON-RPC.
That stands for JavaScript Object Notation Remote Procedure Call.
A protocol error is a JSON-RPC error object.
It's for an unknown tool name, a malformed request, or a server fault.
The second kind is a tool execution error.
It comes back inside a normal, successful result, with the isError flag set to true, plus actionable prose.
That covers upstream service failures, input validation, business rules, and permission denials.
The M C P specification states the consequence directly.
Execution errors carry actionable feedback the model can use to correct itself, and retry with adjusted parameters.
Protocol errors describe problems with the request structure that models are less likely to fix.
So how do you decide the channel?
Carry this rule into the exam.
If a well-formed call reached your logic, and your logic decided the answer, it's an execution error, returned as a result.
If the call never made sense as a call, it's a protocol error.
One spelling note, so it doesn't look like a typo.
On the M C P wire, the flag is isError, in camel case, on the result.
In the Messages application programming interface, the tool_result block uses is_error, with an underscore.
Same idea.
Two surfaces.
Both correct where they appear.
Question one.
This one is select two.
Here's the scenario.
A refund service reports most failures as results with isError set to true.
The team adopts the rule that anything a well-formed call reached belongs in the result.
Which two belong in the JSON-RPC protocol error channel instead?
Take a second.
The answers.
First, the client invoking a tool name the server has never registered.
Second, a request so malformed the server cannot parse it as a tool call.
Neither one reached tool logic.
Now the wrong turns.
All three distractors reached the server's logic.
Wrong: an upstream payments service returning a five-oh-three, service unavailable.
Why?
That's a transient execution error, with a retry hint.
Wrong: a refund rejected because the order shipped outside the ninety-day window.
Why?
That's a legitimate business outcome of a well-formed call.
Wrong: a service account missing write scope.
Why?
That's a permission outcome.
It's returned as a non-retryable result, telling the agent to stop and escalate.
The study notes add a worked version of the business case.
A payments server returns a refund outside the window as a JSON-RPC error.
It says only "refund failed."
The agent retries four or five times.
Then it tells the customer the payment system is down.
What's the fix?
A result with isError true.
Prose saying the order shipped ninety-four days ago, against a ninety-day window.
An instruction not to retry.
And the name of the goodwill-credit tool to use instead.
Now the wrong turns.
Watch these neighbouring distractors.
Wrong: relabel it as an invalid-parameters protocol error.
Why?
The request was not malformed.
Wrong: return isError false, with the rejection as text.
Why?
That presents a failure as success.
And it invites the agent to report a refund that never happened.
Wrong: stuff the policy document into a protocol error's data field.
Why?
It still uses the channel the model cannot act on.
Hold on to this line.
If your logic decided it, it's a result with isError true.
If the call never made sense, it's a protocol error.
Second concept.
The silent failure.
That's the story from the cold open.
Picture asking a colleague to check the stockroom.
They come back saying "nothing there."
But actually, the door was locked.
So you cancel the order you should have chased.
"I couldn't get in, try again in ten minutes" is a completely different message.
And it leads to the right next step.
Question two.
Here's the scenario. order_search returns an empty list in two situations.
When a customer genuinely has no orders.
And when the database times out.
During an incident, the agent told dozens of customers they had no orders.
The team wants outages handled correctly, without retrying genuinely empty results.
What should order_search return on a timeout?
Take a second.
The answer.
A result with isError true, stating a transient timeout that is retryable, with a short retry hint.
Meanwhile, genuine zero matches stay as a plain empty list, with no error flag.
The dedicated flag separates failure from a legitimately empty answer.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: keep the empty list, and add a prompt rule to retry twice on every empty result.
Why?
It still can't tell the two cases apart.
It retries every genuine empty result, which the stem explicitly does not want.
And it still misreports a long outage as no orders.
Wrong: throw an uncaught exception, so the pipeline stops.
Why?
It leaves the model with no context and no recovery path.
That's the all-or-nothing anti-pattern.
Wrong: return a JSON-RPC protocol error.
Why?
It treats an upstream timeout, which is an execution failure, as a malformed request.
And it strips the text the model uses to recover.
The constraint phrase to listen for is "without retrying genuinely empty results."
It rules out any answer that cannot distinguish the two cases.
Hold on to this line.
An empty list on failure is a lie.
Mark failures as failures.
Third concept.
The four classes of execution error.
This is the vocabulary the whole exam reuses.
One.
Transient.
That means a timeout, a rate limit, an upstream server error, or a reset connection.
The agent should retry the same call, within a bound, then report.
The payload says retryable is true, and carries a retry hint.
Two.
Validation.
The input was wrong.
So the agent fixes the input, or escalates.
Three.
Business.
The call was valid, and the answer is no, like the refund window.
It's not retryable.
The payload names the rule and an alternative path, often in a field called next_action.
Why?
Because the parameters were never the problem, so changing them cannot help.
Four.
Permission.
This caller may not do this.
It's not retryable.
The payload names the required scope, and the agent stops and escalates to a person.
The system audits the attempt.
And scope is never widened automatically.
Picture a courier, told at reception that only the named recipient can sign for a parcel.
If the note just says "didn't work, try again," they come back six times, and annoy everyone.
If it says "only the recipient can sign, go back to the sender," they stop after one visit.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A research subagent calls fetch_filing on a licensed financial database.
For filings outside the subscription, the server returns isError true, with the text "Request failed, please try again."
The subagent retries each one six times, exhausting its budget.
And the provider's audit log flags hundreds of denied requests.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Classify it as a non-retryable permission error.
One that names the missing entitlement, and tells the agent to stop.
Now the wrong turns.
They're instructive.
Wrong: lower the retry cap from six to two.
Why?
That treats the symptom.
Two retries of a denial are still two wasted calls, and two audit entries.
The principle behind this is one of the most quotable on the exam.
Hold on to this line.
Classification overrides the retry counter.
A failure classified as non-retryable is never retried, however much budget remains.
Wrong: return the denial as a JSON-RPC error.
Why?
It makes it read as a server fault.
And that invites more retries, not fewer.
Wrong: have the server silently leave unsubscribed filings out of its results.
Why?
That's the silent-failure pattern again.
The coordinator can't tell coverage is incomplete.
So it reports partial research as complete.
The gap must reach the coordinator, not disappear.
Now the mirror image, from the notes.
A server calls a geocoding service, which returns a four twenty-nine, too many requests.
The server returns isError true, with the text "geocoding unavailable."
Agents respond by switching to a worse text-search fallback.
And they never retry the geocoder, even though the limit clears in seconds.
Here, the error is under-signalled, in the other direction.
The fix keeps isError true.
It states that it's a transient rate limit.
It tells the agent to retry the same call after a short pause.
And it puts a retry hint and a correlation identifier in the structured payload.
Wrong: remove the fallback tool.
Why?
That punishes the agent for a signalling defect on the server.
So the same design principle cuts both ways.
A denial written as "try again" causes endless retries.
A transient failure written as "unavailable" causes premature giving up.
Hold on to this line.
Transient means retry within a bound.
Business means change the plan.
Permission means stop and escalate.
Fourth concept.
Two readers of one error.
Picture a hospital chart.
It has a handwritten note for the next nurse.
And a coloured sticker on the cover, for the porter who moves patients.
The porter doesn't read handwriting to decide where to go.
They read the sticker.
Remove the note, and the nurse is lost.
Remove the sticker, and the porter is guessing.
In technical terms, the result carries two things.
A content block, with prose for the model.
And a structuredContent object, with machine-readable fields for your orchestration code.
The fields the sources name are error_class, retryable, retry_after_seconds, upstream, and correlation_id.
And for business and permission errors, things like rule, next_action, and required_scope.
Why both?
The prose is for the model, which reasons in language.
The classification is for code, which needs a stable field to branch on.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
An extraction pipeline's orchestrator must decide, for every failed document, whether to requeue it, send it to a person, or drop it.
Today, failures come back as prose only.
The orchestrator parses the text with regular expressions, which break whenever a message is reworded.
The model's own recovery from the prose works well.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Keep the prose in the content block.
And add error_class, retryable and a retry hint in structuredContent.
Now the wrong turns.
Each one breaks one of the two readers.
Wrong: standardise the wording, and keep the regular expressions.
Why?
It leaves the orchestrator coupled to phrasing.
So the next rewording breaks it again.
Wrong: move every failure to JSON-RPC errors with numeric codes.
Why?
It gives code something to switch on.
But it strips the text the model recovers from.
Wrong: replace the prose with a compact JSON block.
Why?
It drops the explanatory sentence the model uses to choose its next step.
The constraint phrase here is "without hurting the model."
That tells you the prose must survive.
This connects to a cross-cutting principle.
One vocabulary across layers.
The same error_class values, transient, business and permission, are reused by subagent failure reports.
So a coordinator routes on a single taxonomy.
You'll meet that again in the chapter on agentic architecture and orchestration.
Hold on to this line.
Prose for the model, structured fields for the code, and never make either read the other's.
Fifth concept.
Where recovery should happen, in a multi-agent system.
Picture a member of a survey team who finds a shop closed for lunch.
Do they phone the manager, who then cancels the whole survey?
No.
They wait ten minutes, and try again.
They only call in if the shop stays shut.
And even then, the manager keeps everyone else's completed forms.
Question five.
Here's the scenario.
A research subagent's web fetch occasionally times out.
Today, it returns the raw failure to the coordinator on the first timeout.
And the coordinator aborts the whole research run, discarding findings the other subagents already returned.
The timeouts usually clear within seconds.
What's the best change?
Take a second.
The answer.
The subagent retries transient failures locally, with a bound.
And it escalates a structured error only when retries run out.
The coordinator then merges the partial findings, and carries the gap into the final report.
Something like "eleven of twelve sources covered."
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: have the coordinator re-run every failed fetch itself.
Why?
It pushes work up to an agent that then duplicates the subagent, costing context and turns.
Wrong: raise the subagent's turn cap.
Why?
That's a global remedy for a missing policy.
The subagent isn't short of turns.
It lacks a recovery rule.
Wrong: return an empty result on timeout.
Why?
That's the silent failure again.
So the coordinator reports incomplete research as complete.
Hold on to this line.
Recover locally, escalate with structure, and never let one failure sink the run.
Quick recap.
When does an agent retry, when does it change plan, and when does it stop?
Not when a counter says so.
The class decides.
Transient.
Retry within a bound.
Business.
Change the plan, using the named alternative.
Permission.
Stop and escalate.
Protocol.
Fix the client or the server, because there's little the model can do.
And the anti-patterns the notes name.
There are three.
Generic "try again" messages.
Business or permission outcomes sent as protocol errors.
And isError false on a failure.
That's part two.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
The class of the failure decides what happens next.
So say it clearly, in words for the model, and in fields for the code.
Coming up in part three: distributing tools across agents, and configuring tool choice.
